Smooth affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}

Buddhadev Hajra Address: Stat-Math Unit, Indian Statistical Institute Kolkata, 203 B. T. Road, Baranagar, Kolkata 700108, India Email address: hajrabuddhadev92@gmail.com
Abstract.

We classify smooth complex affine surfaces admitting a finite surjective morphism from 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Using the classification theory of smooth affine surfaces according to logarithmic Kodaira dimension, we show that every such surface has logarithmic Kodaira dimension either −∞-\infty or 00, and determine all possibilities. More precisely, the only surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension −∞-\infty are 𝐂2\mathbf{C}^{2} and 𝐂×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, while those of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 00 are precisely 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} and Fujita’s surface H⁡[−1,0,−1]H[-1,0,-1]. This establishes the classification of smooth affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} anticipated by M. Furushima in 1989.

Key words and phrases:
Affine surface, finite morphism, logarithmic Kodaira dimension, Eilenberg–MacLane space

1. Introduction

Throughout, all algebraic varieties and morphisms are defined over the field of complex numbers 𝐂\mathbf{C}.

An algebraic variety VV is said to be properly dominated by an algebraic variety WW if there exists a proper surjective morphism φ:W→V\varphi\colon W\rightarrow V. Since proper morphisms between affine varieties are finite, if VV and WW are affine, this is equivalent to requiring that φ\varphi be finite and surjective. Equivalently, writing V=Spec⁡AV=\Spec A and W=Spec⁡BW=\Spec B, where AA and BB are finitely generated 𝐂\mathbf{C}-algebras, proper domination is equivalent to BB being integral (or, equivalently, finite) over AA.

A fundamental source of examples is provided by Noether normalization, which asserts that every affine variety of dimension dd admits a finite surjective morphism onto the affine space 𝐀d\mathbf{A}^{d}. Thus every affine variety properly dominates the affine space of the same dimension.

The problem becomes considerably subtler when the dominating variety is fixed and one seeks to determine the resulting geometric or structural restrictions on the target. This question has long been an important theme in affine algebraic geometry. For affine surfaces, it is closely related to affine fibrations, the logarithmic Kodaira dimension, and the geometry of the boundary divisor in a suitable log-smooth completion.

Normal affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂2\mathbf{C}^{2} have been extensively studied by Miyanishi, Gurjar, Shastri, Furushima, and others (see, for example, [21, 22] for algebro-geometric proofs and [12, 10, 11] for topological proofs). Furushima subsequently investigated an analytic analogue of this problem by replacing finite surjective algebraic morphisms by proper holomorphic maps from 𝐂2\mathbf{C}^{2} to normal complex analytic surfaces admitting analytic compactifications11 1 A normal complex analytic surface XX is said to admit an analytic compactification if there exist a normal compact complex surface X¯\bar{X} and an analytic subset Z⊆X¯Z\subseteq\bar{X} such that X¯∖Z\bar{X}\setminus Z is biholomorphic to XX. [5]. He later studied normal affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} [6]. The next natural problem is therefore to classify affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Furushima’s analysis of the 𝐂×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} case relies heavily on the Nishino–Suzuki theorem on cluster sets of holomorphic mappings from a punctured disc into a smooth compact complex surface, together with Suzuki’s study of analytic compactifications of 𝐂×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Using these techniques, Furushima remarked that analogous methods should yield a classification of normal affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, namely

𝐂2,𝐂×𝐂∗,𝐂∗×𝐂∗,\mathbf{C}^{2},\qquad\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{C}^{*},\qquad\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*},

and suitable finite quotients of these surfaces by subgroups of G​L​(2,𝐂)GL(2,\mathbf{C}) (see [6, Remark]). Although Furushima indicated that the details would appear elsewhere, to the best of the author’s knowledge no complete proof has subsequently appeared in the literature.

The objective of the present article is to establish the classification of smooth affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, thereby confirming Furushima’s prediction in the smooth case. Our approach is entirely different from Furushima’s analytic methods. Instead, it relies on recent advances in the theory of open algebraic surfaces, most notably the classification of smooth non-contractible affine Eilenberg–MacLane K⁡(π,1)K(\pi,1)-surfaces established in [9, Result 2.1].

The main result of this article is the following.

Theorem A (Theorems 12 and 18).

Let YY be a smooth affine surface properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Then κ¯​(Y)∈{−∞,0}\bar{\kappa}(Y)\in\{-\infty,0\}, and the following assertions hold.

  1. (1)

    If κ¯​(Y)=−∞\bar{\kappa}(Y)=-\infty, then

    Y≅𝐂2orY≅𝐂×𝐂∗.Y\cong\mathbf{C}^{2}\quad\text{or}\quad Y\cong\mathbf{C}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.
  2. (2)

    If κ¯​(Y)=0\bar{\kappa}(Y)=0, then

    Y≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗orY≅H⁡[−1,0,−1].Y\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}\quad\text{or}\quad Y\cong H[-1,0,-1].

The appearance of the surface H⁡[−1,0,−1]H[-1,0,-1], introduced by Fujita [4], is particularly noteworthy. It was proved in [9, Proposition 5.8] that H⁡[−1,0,−1]H[-1,0,-1] admits a finite étale double cover

π:𝐂∗×𝐂∗→H⁡[−1,0,−1].\pi\colon\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}\rightarrow H[-1,0,-1].

Since every connected double cover is Galois, the deck transformation group Deck⁡(π)\operatorname{Deck}(\pi) is isomorphic to 𝐙/2​𝐙\mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z}. Hence there exists a fixed-point-free involution σ∈Aut⁡(𝐂∗×𝐂∗)\sigma\in\Aut(\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}) such that

Deck⁡(π)=⟨σ⟩andH⁡[−1,0,−1]≅(𝐂∗×𝐂∗)/⟨σ⟩.\operatorname{Deck}(\pi)=\langle\sigma\rangle\quad\text{and}\quad H[-1,0,-1]\cong(\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*})/\langle\sigma\rangle.

Thus Theorem A confirms Furushima’s predicted classification in the smooth setting.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we collect the preliminary material used throughout the paper. Besides fixing notation and conventions, we recall the Suzuki–Zaidenberg formula for the topological Euler characteristic of smooth affine surfaces admitting affine fibrations, several auxiliary results on affine fibrations and finite morphisms, the theory of the fundamental group at infinity of normal algebraic surfaces due to Mumford and its extension by Wagreich, and the class 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} of smooth factorial affine surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero with trivial units. Section 3 contains the proofs of the main results. We first establish the case κ¯=−∞\bar{\kappa}=-\infty by proving Theorem 12. We then develop several auxiliary results on finite étale covers of complements of finite subsets of 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} and on certain classes of affine surfaces that cannot be properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. These ingredients are combined in the final part of the section to prove Theorem 18.

2. Preliminaries

We begin by fixing notation and conventions that will be used throughout the article.

We now recall some well-known results that will frequently be used in the subsequent sections.

2.2. Suzuki–Zaidenberg formula for the topological Euler-Poincaré characteristic

M. Suzuki proved an important formula for the Euler–Poincaré characteristic of a smooth affine surface fibered over a smooth algebraic curve (cf. [29]).

Theorem 1 (Suzuki–Zaidenberg Formula; cf. [29, 32]).

Let f:V→Cf\colon V\rightarrow C be a surjective morphism from a smooth affine surface VV onto a smooth algebraic curve CC such that a general fiber FF of ff is irreducible. Let p1,…,pnp_{1},\ldots,p_{n} be the points of CC at which ff is not 𝒞∞\mathscr{C}^{\infty}-locally trivial. Then

e⁡(V)=e⁡(C)⋅e⁡(F)+∑i=1n(e⁡(Fi)−e⁡(F)),e(V)=e(C)\cdot e(F)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(e(F_{i})-e(F)\bigr),

where Fi:=f−1​(pi)F_{i}:=f^{-1}(p_{i}) for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

Moreover, each summand e⁡(Fi)−e⁡(F)e(F_{i})-e(F) is non-negative. If e⁡(Fi)=e⁡(F)e(F_{i})=e(F) for some ii, then FF is isomorphic to either 𝐂\mathbf{C} or 𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{\ast}, and (Fi)red(F_{i})_{\mathrm{red}} is isomorphic to FF.

Here, the last part about the non-negativity of every summand appearing in the above formula was essentially due to M. Zaidenberg (cf. [32]). The proofs in [29] and [32] use the theory of plurisubharmonic functions. A more algebro-geometric approach to the proof of this result was later given by R. V. Gurjar (cf. [13]).

2.3. Some useful assorted results

The following result is well-known. For the sake of completeness, we add a short proof. This result will be used in subsequent proofs.

Lemma 2.

Let f:X→Bf\colon X\rightarrow B be an FF-fibration from a smooth affine surface XX onto a smooth algebraic curve BB, where FF is a smooth affine rational curve. If ρ⁡(X)=0\rho(X)=0, then the following holds.

  1. (1)

    BB is affine.

  2. (2)

    All fibers of ff are irreducible.

Proof.

Let f:X→Bf\colon X\rightarrow B be an FF-fibration from a smooth affine surface XX with ρ⁡(X)=0\rho(X)=0 onto a smooth algebraic curve BB. Let X⊆VX\subseteq V be an open embedding into a smooth projective surface VV such that ff extends to a ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}-fibration φ:V→B¯\varphi\colon V\rightarrow\bar{B} over a smooth projective curve B¯\bar{B}, where B⊆B¯B\subseteq\bar{B} is the smooth completion.

Since ρ⁡(X)=0\rho(X)=0, Pic⁡(V)\Pic(V) is finitely generated. Consequently, using the Hodge theory and the long exact cohomology sequence induced from the exponential sequence of analytic sheaves, it follows that b1​(V)=0b_{1}(V)=0. As a general fiber of φ\varphi is isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}, which is connected, the induced homomorphism

φ∗:H1​(V,𝐙)→H1​(B¯,𝐙)\varphi_{\ast}\colon H_{1}(V;\mathbf{Z})\rightarrow H_{1}(\bar{B};\mathbf{Z})

is surjective. Hence b1​(B¯)≤b1​(V)=0b_{1}(\bar{B})\leq b_{1}(V)=0, which implies that B¯≅ℙ1\bar{B}\cong\mathbb{P}^{1} and thus BB is rational.

Since B¯≅ℙ1\bar{B}\cong\mathbb{P}^{1}, one general fiber of φ\varphi, a cross-section of φ\varphi, and the compactifications (in VV) of all but one irreducible component of each singular fiber of ff freely generate Pic⁡(V)\Pic(V).

If B=ℙ1B=\mathbb{P}^{1}, it follows that one general fiber of ff and all but one irreducible component of each singular fiber of ff freely generate Pic⁡(X)\Pic(X). Thus, ρ⁡(X)=rank𝐙⁡Pic⁡(X)≥1\rho(X)=\rank_{\mathbf{Z}}\Pic(X)\geq 1, which contradicts the assumption that ρ⁡(X)=0\rho(X)=0. Hence BB must be affine, proving (1).

Now let BB be a smooth affine rational curve. From the above description of the free generators of Pic⁡(V)\Pic(V), it follows that all but one irreducible component of each singular fiber of ff freely generate Pic⁡(X)\Pic(X). Therefore, ρ⁡(X)=rank𝐙⁡Pic⁡(X)≥1\rho(X)=\rank_{\mathbf{Z}}\Pic(X)\geq 1 whenever ff has a reducible fiber. This would again contradict the assumption that ρ⁡(X)=0\rho(X)=0. Hence, all fibers of ff are irreducible, proving (2). ∎

Now we will quote two useful results from [18].

Lemma 3 (cf. [18, Lemma 2.6, Corollary 2.7]).

Let XX be a smooth quasi-projective surface and π:X→B\pi\colon X\rightarrow B a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle over a smooth algebraic curve BB. Then the following holds.

  1. (1)

    There exists a finite étale cover B′→BB^{\prime}\rightarrow B of degree at most 22 inducing a finite étale cover X′:=X×BB′→XX^{\prime}:=X\times_{B}B^{\prime}\rightarrow X such that X′→B′X^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime} is an untwisted 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle.

  2. (2)

    The logarithmic Kodaira dimensions satisfy

    κ¯​(X′)=κ¯​(X)=κ¯​(B)=κ¯​(B′).\bar{\kappa}(X^{\prime})=\bar{\kappa}(X)=\bar{\kappa}(B)=\bar{\kappa}(B^{\prime}).
  3. (3)

    If π\pi is untwisted and BB is a smooth affine rational curve, then π\pi is a trivial 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle.

  4. (4)

    If XX is a smooth affine surface and π\pi is a 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{m}-bundle, then BB is affine.

Lemma 4 (cf. [18, Lemma 2.14]).

Any 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}-bundle over a smooth affine rational curve is trivial.

Now we list certain results that are used repeatedly in the context of proper descent of algebraic varieties.

Lemma 5.

Let f:V→Wf\colon V\rightarrow W be a finite surjective morphism between smooth, irreducible complex algebraic varieties. Then the following holds.

  1. (1)

    κ¯​(V)≥κ¯​(W)\bar{\kappa}(V)\geq\bar{\kappa}(W). Moreover, if ff is étale, then κ¯​(V)=κ¯​(W)\bar{\kappa}(V)=\bar{\kappa}(W) (cf. [17]).

  2. (2)

    The induced homomorphism

    f∗:Hi​(V,𝐐)→Hi​(W,𝐐)f_{\ast}:H_{i}(V;\mathbf{Q})\rightarrow H_{i}(W;\mathbf{Q})

    is surjective for all ii. In particular, bi​(V)≥bi​(W)b_{i}(V)\geq b_{i}(W) for all ii (cf. [8]).

  3. (3)

    There is an induced injective homomorphism (by the projection formula)

    f∗⊗Id𝐐:Pic⁡(W)⊗𝐙𝐐→Pic⁡(V)⊗𝐙𝐐.f^{\ast}\otimes\mathrm{Id}_{\mathbf{Q}}\colon\Pic(W)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}\rightarrow\Pic(V)\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{Q}.

    In particular, ρ⁡(W)≤ρ⁡(V)\rho(W)\leq\rho(V).

2.4. 33-manifold at infinity and π1∞\pi_{1}^{\infty} of normal affine surfaces

Let XX be a normal affine surface over 𝐂\mathbf{C}. By resolution of singularities, there exists a smooth projective surface VV containing XX as a dense Zariski open subset such that D:=V∖XD:=V\setminus X is a connected simple normal crossing divisor (SNC divisor, for short). The pair (V,D)(V,D) is called a log-smooth completion of XX.

Regard VV as a complex analytic manifold equipped with its Euclidean topology. For a sufficiently small positive real number ε\varepsilon, let Nε​(D)N_{\varepsilon}(D) denote the tubular neighbourhood of DD consisting of all points whose distance from DD is at most ε\varepsilon. Then DD is a strong deformation retract of Nε​(D)N_{\varepsilon}(D), and the boundary MX:=∂Nε​(D)M_{X}:=\partial N_{\varepsilon}(D) is a compact connected orientable 𝒞∞\mathscr{C}^{\infty}-smooth 33-manifold. Moreover, MXM_{X} is a strong deformation retract of the punctured tubular neighbourhood Nε​(D)∖DN_{\varepsilon}(D)\setminus D. The manifold MXM_{X} is called the 33-manifold at infinity of XX.

Mumford [23] showed that MXM_{X} is naturally realized as the plumbing manifold associated with the weighted dual graph of the boundary divisor DD. In particular, MXM_{X} is a graph manifold in the sense of Waldhausen [31]. We refer the reader to Eisenbud and Neumann [2] for a detailed treatment of graph manifolds, their plumbing descriptions, and their relation to the JSJ decomposition.

Recall that a connected 33-manifold MM is called prime if, whenever M=M1​#​M2M=M_{1}\#M_{2}, one of the summands M1M_{1} or M2M_{2} is homeomorphic to the 33-sphere S3S^{3}. It is called irreducible if every smoothly embedded 22-sphere in MM bounds a 33-ball. By a theorem of W. D. Neumann [25, Theorem 5.1], the 33-manifold at infinity MXM_{X} is prime. Furthermore, every connected orientable prime 33-manifold is either irreducible or homeomorphic to S2×S1S^{2}\times S^{1} (see [16, Lemma 3.13]).

The fundamental group at infinity of XX is defined by π1∞​(X):=π1​(MX)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X):=\pi_{1}(M_{X}), or equivalently, as the fundamental group of the boundary of a sufficiently small tubular neighbourhood of the boundary divisor DD. This group is independent of the choice of ε\varepsilon, provided that ε\varepsilon is sufficiently small, and also independent of the chosen log-smooth completion (see, for example, [14, before Theorem 1.2.11]).

The fundamental group at infinity admits an intrinsic topological description in terms of complements of compact subsets of XX. Indeed, let K1⊆K2⊆⋯K_{1}\subseteq K_{2}\subseteq\cdots be an exhaustion of XX by compact subsets such that X=⋃i=1∞KiX=\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty}K_{i}. Then, for every i≤ji\leq j, the inclusion ηi​j:X∖Kj↪X∖Ki\eta_{ij}\colon X\setminus K_{j}\hookrightarrow X\setminus K_{i} induces a homomorphism (ηi​j)∗:π1​(X∖Kj)→π1​(X∖Ki)(\eta_{ij})_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X\setminus K_{j})\rightarrow\pi_{1}(X\setminus K_{i}). Moreover, ηi​i=idX∖Ki\eta_{ii}=\id_{X\setminus K_{i}} for each ii, and ηi​k=ηi​j∘ηj​k\eta_{ik}=\eta_{ij}\circ\eta_{jk} for all i≤j≤ki\leq j\leq k. Thus, {(π1​(X∖Ki))i∈𝐍,((ηi​j)∗)i≤j∈𝐍}\{(\pi_{1}(X\setminus K_{i}))_{i\in\mathbf{N}},((\eta_{ij})_{\ast})_{i\leq j\in\mathbf{N}}\} forms an inverse system of groups and transition morphisms over the poset (𝐍,⊆)(\mathbf{N},\subseteq), and

π1∞​(X)≅lim←i⁡π1​(X∖Ki).\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X)\cong\varprojlim_{i}\pi_{1}(X\setminus K_{i}).

This inverse limit is independent of the chosen exhaustion of XX.

2.4.1. Mumford’s presentation for rational tree boundary divisors

We recall a presentation of the fundamental group at infinity due to Mumford [23, §1.2] (see also [14, §1.3.9]). More generally, Mumford described the fundamental group of the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood of a compact, connected divisor with simple normal crossings on a 22-dimensional complex manifold, provided that its dual graph has no non-trivial loops. The presentation depends on the intersection matrix of the divisor and the genera of its irreducible components. Since we shall only need the case where every irreducible component of the divisor is a smooth rational curve, we record only this special case.

Let XX be a normal affine surface, and let (V,D)(V,D) be a log-smooth completion of XX. Assume that the connected boundary divisor D=D1+⋯+DnD=D_{1}+\cdots+D_{n} has smooth rational irreducible components and that its dual graph Γ=Γ⁡(D)\Gamma=\Gamma(D) is a tree. Let si​j:=(Di⋅Dj)s_{ij}:=(D_{i}\cdot D_{j}) denote the entries of the intersection matrix of DD. Note that si​j=0​ or ​1s_{ij}=0\text{ or }1 if i≠ji\neq j and si​i<0s_{ii}<0 for all 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n. For each irreducible component DiD_{i}, let eie_{i} denote the corresponding meridian generator of π1∞​(X)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X). If εi\varepsilon_{i} is the vertex of Γ\Gamma, corresponding to DiD_{i} then we shall say that eie_{i} is the generator of π1∞​(X)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X) corresponding to εi\varepsilon_{i}.

Proposition 6 (Mumford, cf. [23]).

With the above notation,

π1∞(X)=⟨e1,…,en|∏j=1nejsi​j=1for each i=1,…,n,and [ei,ej]=1whenever Di∩Dj≠∅⟩.\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X)=\Bigl\langle e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}\ \Big|\ \prod_{j=1}^{n}e_{j}^{\,s_{ij}}=1\ \text{for each }i=1,\ldots,n,\ \text{and }\ [e_{i},e_{j}]=1\ \text{whenever }D_{i}\cap D_{j}\neq\varnothing\Bigr\rangle.

2.4.2. Wagreich’s presentation for rational unicyclic boundary divisors

We now recall a generalization of Mumford’s presentation due to Wagreich [30, Proposition 2.2]. More generally, Wagreich described the fundamental group at infinity of a smooth affine surface whose boundary divisor has a dual graph containing a unique cycle. Since this is the only case needed later, we record the corresponding presentation.

Let XX be a smooth affine surface, and let (V,D)(V,D) be a log-smooth completion of XX. Assume that the dual graph Γ=Γ⁡(D)\Gamma=\Gamma(D) has a unique cycle and no centres. Choose a vertex ε0\varepsilon_{0} on the unique cycle of Γ\Gamma. Let Γ1,…,Γs\Gamma_{1},\ldots,\Gamma_{s} be the connected components of Γ−{ε0}\Gamma-\{\varepsilon_{0}\}, and assume that Γ1\Gamma_{1} contains the unique cycle. Let ε1,…,εr\varepsilon_{1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{r} be the vertices of Γ1\Gamma_{1} and let εr+1,…,εt\varepsilon_{r+1},\ldots,\varepsilon_{t} denote the remaining vertices of Γ\Gamma. 3. Proof of the Main Theorem

Let YY be a smooth affine surface properly dominated by the complex algebraic 22-torus X=𝐂∗×𝐂∗X=\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Our goal is to determine all possible isomorphism classes of YY.

A recurring feature of our arguments is that many geometric and topological properties are preserved under finite étale coverings. Consequently, it is convenient to first replace YY, whenever necessary, by a suitable finite étale cover so that the induced homomorphism on fundamental groups becomes surjective. This reduction will simplify the subsequent arguments and will be invoked repeatedly throughout the proofs.

We begin by recording this elementary but useful observation.

Remark 1 (Reduction to the surjective fundamental group case).

Let f:X→Yf\colon X\rightarrow Y be a finite surjective morphism between smooth affine varieties. We first reduce to the case where the induced homomorphism f∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Y)f_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Y) is surjective.

Suppose that f∗f_{\ast} is not surjective. Since the image f∗​(π1​(X))f_{\ast}(\pi_{1}(X)) has finite index in π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) by a theorem of Serre (cf. [27]), covering space theory yields a connected finite étale covering g:Z→Yg\colon Z\rightarrow Y corresponding to the subgroup f∗​(π1​(X))⊆π1​(Y)f_{\ast}(\pi_{1}(X))\subseteq\pi_{1}(Y). Consequently, ff admits the following factorization:

where h:X→Zh\colon X\rightarrow Z is again a finite surjective morphism satisfying f=g∘hf=g\circ h. Moreover, g∗​(π1​(Z))=f∗​(π1​(X))g_{\ast}\bigl(\pi_{1}(Z)\bigr)=f_{\ast}\bigl(\pi_{1}(X)\bigr), and hence h∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Z)h_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Z) is surjective. Furthermore, deg⁡(f)=deg⁡(g)​deg⁡(h)\deg(f)=\deg(g)\deg(h).

Therefore, after replacing YY by the finite étale covering ZZ, we may always assume that the induced homomorphism on fundamental groups is surjective. This reduction will be invoked repeatedly throughout the proofs in this section.

The above reduction enables us to replace the target surface by a suitable finite étale covering whenever necessary, without changing its smoothness or logarithmic Kodaira dimension. The following result describes the connected finite étale coverings of the complement of a finite subset of 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}. It will play a fundamental role throughout the remainder of this section, since it guarantees that every connected finite étale cover of 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2} is again isomorphic to 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}.

Proposition 11.

Let S={p1,…,pk}⊆𝔾m2S=\{p_{1},\ldots,p_{k}\}\subseteq\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2} be a finite subset, where k≥0k\geq 0, and let S=∅S=\varnothing when k=0k=0. Suppose that

φ:V→𝔾m2∖S\varphi\colon V\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\setminus S

is a connected finite étale morphism. Then there exists a finite étale endomorphism

Φ:𝔾m2→𝔾m2\Phi\colon\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}

such that V≅𝔾m2∖Φ−1​(S)V\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\setminus\Phi^{-1}(S). In particular, when S=∅S=\varnothing, we have V≅𝔾m2V\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}.

Proof.

Let WW be the normalization of 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2} in the function field 𝐂⁡(V)\mathbf{C}(V) of VV. Then WW is a normal affine surface containing VV as a Zariski open subset, and the finite morphism φ\varphi extends uniquely to a finite surjective morphism

φ¯:W→𝔾m2.\overline{\varphi}\colon W\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}.

Since φ\varphi is étale, the morphism φ¯\overline{\varphi} is unramified over 𝔾m2∖S\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\setminus S. Hence every irreducible component of the branch locus of φ¯\overline{\varphi} is contained in SS. As SS has codimension 22 in 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}, the Zariski–Nagata purity theorem implies that the branch locus of φ¯\overline{\varphi} is empty. Therefore φ¯\overline{\varphi} is unramified. Since 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2} is smooth, WW is a normal algebraic surface (hence Cohen–Macaulay), and φ¯\overline{\varphi} is finite (hence equidimensional), Serre’s miracle flatness implies that φ¯\overline{\varphi} is flat. As it is already unramified, it follows that φ¯\overline{\varphi} is étale. Since every étale morphism is smooth, it follows that WW is smooth.

Passing to the associated complex analytic spaces, we obtain a connected finite-sheeted analytic covering

φ¯an:Wan→(𝔾m2)an=𝐂∗×𝐂∗.\overline{\varphi}^{\rm an}\colon W^{\rm an}\rightarrow(\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2})^{\textrm{an}}=\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Since π1​(𝐂∗×𝐂∗)≅𝐙2\pi_{1}(\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*})\cong\mathbf{Z}^{2}, the covering φ¯an\overline{\varphi}^{\rm an} corresponds to the finite-index subgroup

H=φ¯∗an​(π1​(Wan))⊆𝐙2.H=\overline{\varphi}^{\rm an}_{*}\bigl(\pi_{1}(W^{\rm an})\bigr)\subseteq\mathbf{Z}^{2}.

As HH is a free abelian group of rank 22, choose a 𝐙\mathbf{Z}-basis of HH. If the corresponding basis vectors are the columns of the integer matrix

T=(abcd),det(T)≠0,T=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det(T)\neq 0,

then H=T⁡(𝐙2)H=T(\mathbf{Z}^{2}). Consider the associated monomial endomorphism

Φ:𝔾m2→𝔾m2,(z,w)⟼(za​wb,zc​wd).\Phi\colon\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2},\qquad(z,w)\longmapsto(z^{a}w^{b},z^{c}w^{d}).

It is well known that Φ\Phi is a connected finite étale endomorphism satisfying

Φ∗an​(π1​(𝐂∗×𝐂∗))=H.\Phi^{\rm an}_{*}\bigl(\pi_{1}(\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*})\bigr)=H.

Hence, by the classification of connected covering spaces, φ¯an\overline{\varphi}^{\rm an} and Φan\Phi^{\rm an} are isomorphic as analytic coverings of 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. The Generalized Riemann Existence Theorem then implies that φ¯\overline{\varphi} and Φ\Phi are isomorphic as finite étale covers of 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}. Thus, after identifying WW with 𝔾m2\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}, we may assume that φ¯=Φ\overline{\varphi}=\Phi.

Finally, since φ\varphi is the restriction of φ¯\overline{\varphi} to 𝔾m2∖S\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\setminus S, we obtain

V≅W∖φ¯−1​(S)≅𝔾m2∖Φ−1​(S).V\cong W\setminus\overline{\varphi}^{-1}(S)\cong\mathbb{G}_{m}^{2}\setminus\Phi^{-1}(S).

Since Φ\Phi is finite, the set Φ−1​(S)\Phi^{-1}(S) is finite, completing the proof. ∎

We now proceed to classify smooth affine surfaces properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Since κ¯​(𝐂∗×𝐂∗)=0\bar{\kappa}(\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*})=0 and logarithmic Kodaira dimension does not increase under finite surjective morphisms by Lemma 5(1), we necessarily have κ¯​(Y)≤0\bar{\kappa}(Y)\leq 0. Thus it suffices to consider the two cases κ¯​(Y)=−∞\bar{\kappa}(Y)=-\infty and κ¯​(Y)=0\bar{\kappa}(Y)=0, which we treat separately.

3.1. The case κ¯​(Y)=−∞\bar{\kappa}(Y)=-\infty

Theorem 12.

Let YY be a smooth affine surface with κ¯​(Y)=−∞\bar{\kappa}(Y)=-\infty. If YY is properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, then YY is isomorphic to either 𝐀2\mathbf{A}^{2} or 𝐀1×𝐂∗\mathbf{A}^{1}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Proof.

Let X:=𝐂∗×𝐂∗X:=\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} and let f:X→Yf\colon X\rightarrow Y be a finite surjective morphism. If deg⁡(f)=1\deg(f)=1, then ff is a finite birational morphism and hence an isomorphism by Zariski’s Main Theorem, which cannot occur since κ¯​(X)=0\bar{\kappa}(X)=0 whereas κ¯​(Y)=−∞\bar{\kappa}(Y)=-\infty. Thus deg⁡(f)>1\deg(f)>1.

By Remark 1, we may factorize ff as f=g∘hf=g\circ h, where g:Z→Yg\colon Z\rightarrow Y is a finite étale morphism and h:X→Zh\colon X\rightarrow Z is a finite surjective morphism inducing a surjection h∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Z)h_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Z). Since logarithmic Kodaira dimension is preserved under finite étale coverings by Lemma 5(1), we have κ¯​(Z)=κ¯​(Y)=−∞\bar{\kappa}(Z)=\bar{\kappa}(Y)=-\infty.

By the results of Fujita–Miyanishi–Sugie [3, 20, 28], the surface ZZ admits an 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}-fibration φ:Z→B\varphi\colon Z\rightarrow B over a smooth algebraic curve BB. Furthermore, ρ⁡(Z)=0\rho(Z)=0 by Lemma 5(3), since XX is factorial. Hence Lemma 2 implies that BB is affine and that φ\varphi has no reducible fibers.

Since π1​(X)≅𝐙2\pi_{1}(X)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{2} and h∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Z)h_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Z) is surjective, the group π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is abelian. Moreover, the induced homomorphism φ∗:π1​(Z)→π1​(B)\varphi_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(Z)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(B) is surjective, and therefore π1​(B)\pi_{1}(B) is also abelian. Hence B≅𝐀1B\cong\mathbf{A}^{1} or 𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}.

It remains to show that φ\varphi has no multiple fibers. Suppose, to the contrary, that φ\varphi has a multiple fiber. By the ramified covering trick (cf. [14, Lemma 1.1.9]), there exists a finite morphism B′→BB^{\prime}\rightarrow B inducing a finite étale covering p:Z′→Zp\colon Z^{\prime}\rightarrow Z, where Z′:=Z×BB′¯Z^{\prime}:=\overline{Z\times_{B}B^{\prime}} is the normalization of the fiber product, such that the induced 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}-fibration φ′:Z′→B′\varphi^{\prime}\colon Z^{\prime}\rightarrow B^{\prime} has no multiple fibers. In the process of eliminating multiple fibers, the fibration φ′\varphi^{\prime} necessarily acquires a reducible fiber. Hence ρ⁡(Z′)>0\rho(Z^{\prime})>0 by Lemma 2.

Now let q:V→Xq\colon V\rightarrow X be the pullback of pp via hh. Since h∗h_{\ast} is surjective, VV is connected, and the induced morphism h′:V→Z′h^{\prime}\colon V\rightarrow Z^{\prime} is finite surjective. Moreover, we have the commutative diagram

Since qq is a finite covering, Proposition 11 shows that V≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗V\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Hence Z′Z^{\prime} is again properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Repeating the above argument with Z′Z^{\prime} in place of ZZ, it turns out that ρ⁡(Z′)=0\rho(Z^{\prime})=0, contradicting the existence of a reducible fiber of φ′\varphi^{\prime}. Therefore φ\varphi has no multiple fibers. Since φ\varphi also has no reducible fibers, it follows that φ\varphi is an 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}-bundle. As BB is an affine rational curve, Lemma 4 implies that φ\varphi is trivial.

We now distinguish two cases.

Case 1. B≅𝐀1B\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}.

Then Z≅𝐀2Z\cong\mathbf{A}^{2}. Since gg is a finite topological covering and π1​(Z)=1\pi_{1}(Z)=1, the group π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) is finite. On the other hand, 𝐀2\mathbf{A}^{2} is contractible, so YY is a K⁡(π,1)K(\pi,1)-space. Since YY is an affine surface, it is a finite-dimensional CW complex; therefore π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) is torsion-free using [15, Proposition 2.45], forcing π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) to be trivial. Consequently, gg is an isomorphism, and hence Y≅Z≅𝐀2Y\cong Z\cong\mathbf{A}^{2}.22 2 Aliter. Since Z≅𝐀2Z\cong\mathbf{A}^{2} and YY is the image of ZZ under a finite morphism of smooth affine surfaces, it follows from [21, 10] that Y≅𝐀2Y\cong\mathbf{A}^{2}.

Case 2. B≅𝐂∗B\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Then Z≅𝐀1×𝐂∗Z\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, which is an Eilenberg–MacLane K⁡(π,1)K(\pi,1)-space. Since g:Z→Yg\colon Z\rightarrow Y is a finite topological covering, YY is also an Eilenberg–MacLane K⁡(π,1)K(\pi,1)-space. By [9, Theorem 5.3], YY is an 𝐀1\mathbf{A}^{1}-bundle over a smooth algebraic curve CC. Again, ρ⁡(Y)=0\rho(Y)=0 by Lemma 5(3), since XX is factorial. Hence Lemma 2 implies that CC is affine. Moreover, e⁡(Z)=e⁡(𝐀1×𝐂∗)=0e(Z)=e(\mathbf{A}^{1}\times\mathbf{C}^{*})=0, so e⁡(Y)=0e(Y)=0, and therefore e⁡(C)=0e(C)=0. Thus C≅𝐂∗C\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}, and Lemma 4 shows that Y≅𝐀1×𝐂∗Y\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.33 3 Aliter. Since Z≅𝐀1×𝐂∗Z\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, one may directly apply [6] to conclude that Y≅𝐀1×𝐂∗Y\cong\mathbf{A}^{1}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, as YY is non-contractible because g:Z→Yg\colon Z\rightarrow Y is a finite covering. ∎

3.2. The case κ¯​(Y)=0\bar{\kappa}(Y)=0

Having completed the classification in the case κ¯​(Y)=−∞\bar{\kappa}(Y)=-\infty, we now turn to the remaining case κ¯​(Y)=0\bar{\kappa}(Y)=0. The argument is considerably more subtle. Rather than proceeding directly to the classification, we first establish a sequence of topological and geometric obstructions that progressively eliminate possible fundamental groups and geometric configurations of the target surface YY. These auxiliary results ultimately lead to the classification theorem for smooth affine surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero. The argument proceeds in several steps:

  1. (1)

    We first prove that the fundamental group of YY cannot be finite. A key ingredient is to show that no smooth affine surface in the class 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} can be properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

  2. (2)

    Next, we exclude smooth affine surfaces with an abelian fundamental group of rank 11 and positive Euler characteristic.

  3. (3)

    Finally, combining these obstructions with Kojima’s classification of strongly minimal affine surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero, we obtain the desired classification.

Proposition 13.

Let YY be a smooth affine surface with κ¯​(Y)=0\bar{\kappa}(Y)=0. If YY is properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, then π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) cannot be finite.

Proof.

Let X:=𝐂∗×𝐂∗X:=\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} and let f:X→Yf\colon X\rightarrow Y be a finite surjective morphism. If deg⁡(f)=1\deg(f)=1, then ff is a finite birational morphism between smooth affine surfaces. Hence, by Zariski’s Main Theorem, ff is an isomorphism. This is impossible since π1​(X)≅𝐙2\pi_{1}(X)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{2}, whereas π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) is finite. Therefore, deg⁡(f)>1\deg(f)>1.

Using the reduction in Remark 1, we factorize ff as f=g∘hf=g\circ h, where g:Z→Yg\colon Z\rightarrow Y is a finite étale morphism and h:X→Zh\colon X\rightarrow Z is a finite surjective morphism satisfying h∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Z)h_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Z) is surjective.

Since π1​(X)≅𝐙2\pi_{1}(X)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{2}, the group π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is a finitely generated abelian group. On the other hand, gg is a finite covering, so g∗​(π1​(Z))g_{\ast}(\pi_{1}(Z)) is a finite-index subgroup of the finite group π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y). Consequently, π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is finite.

Let p:Z~→Zp\colon\widetilde{Z}\rightarrow Z be the universal covering. Since π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is finite, the covering pp is finite. Form the fiber product X~:=X×ZZ~\widetilde{X}:=X\times_{Z}\widetilde{Z}. Then we obtain the commutative diagram

Since h∗h_{\ast} is surjective, the pullback q:X~→Xq\colon\widetilde{X}\rightarrow X is connected. Moreover, qq is finite étale, and hence Proposition 11 implies that X~≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗\widetilde{X}\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Therefore, h′:X~→Z~h^{\prime}\colon\widetilde{X}\rightarrow\widetilde{Z} is again a finite surjective morphism.

Since X~\widetilde{X} is factorial, Lemma 5(3) yields ρ⁡(Z~)=0\rho(\widetilde{Z})=0, and consequently Cl⁡(Z~)\Cl(\widetilde{Z}) is finite. As Z~\widetilde{Z} is simply connected, it follows that Z~\widetilde{Z} is in fact factorial and Γ​(Z~,𝒪Z~)∗=𝐂∗\Gamma(\widetilde{Z},\mathcal{O}_{\widetilde{Z}})^{*}=\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Furthermore, since both pp and gg are finite étale morphisms, we have κ¯​(Z~)=κ¯​(Z)=κ¯​(Y)=0\bar{\kappa}(\widetilde{Z})=\bar{\kappa}(Z)=\bar{\kappa}(Y)=0. Hence Z~\widetilde{Z} belongs to the class 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} introduced in §2.5.

The following proposition shows that no surface in 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} can be properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Since X~≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗\widetilde{X}\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} properly dominates Z~\widetilde{Z}, we arrive at a contradiction. Hence no such ff exists. ∎

The preceding proposition reduces the problem to determining whether a surface in the class 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} can be properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. The next proposition shows that this never occurs.

We shall use the following theorem, proved independently by Gabai [7] and Casson–Jungreis [1].

Theorem 14 (Seifert Fiber Space Theorem; cf. [7, 1]).

Let MM be a compact, orientable, irreducible 33-manifold with infinite fundamental group. Then MM is a Seifert fibre space if and only if π1​(M)\pi_{1}(M) contains an infinite cyclic normal subgroup.

Proposition 15.

No smooth affine surface in the class 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} is properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Proof.

Suppose, to the contrary, that there exists a finite surjective morphism f:X→Yf\colon X\rightarrow Y, where X=𝐂∗×𝐂∗X=\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} and Y∈𝒮0Y\in\mathscr{S}_{0}.

Since ff is finite, properness induces a homomorphism f∗∞:π1∞​(X)→π1∞​(Y)f_{\ast}^{\infty}\colon\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y) by [14, Proposition 2.8.8]. Moreover, by Serre’s theorem (cf. [27]), its image has finite index in π1∞​(Y)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y). Suppose that f∗∞f_{\ast}^{\infty} is not surjective. Then, by the factorization argument described in Remark 1, there exists a commutative diagram

where p:S→Yp\colon S\rightarrow Y is a connected finite étale morphism, g:X→Sg\colon X\rightarrow S is a finite surjective morphism, f=p∘gf=p\circ g, and g∗∞:π1∞​(X)→π1∞​(S)g_{\ast}^{\infty}\colon\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}^{\infty}(S) is surjective (see also the proof of [14, Lemma 2.8.5] for details). Since Y∈𝒮0Y\in\mathscr{S}_{0}, it follows from [26, Proposition 4.1] that YY is homotopy equivalent to S2S^{2}, and hence simply connected. Therefore the connected finite étale covering p:S→Yp\colon S\rightarrow Y is trivial, so pp is an isomorphism. Consequently, f∗∞=g∗∞f_{\ast}^{\infty}=g_{\ast}^{\infty} is surjective, a contradiction. Thus f∗∞:π1∞​(X)→π1∞​(Y)f_{\ast}^{\infty}\colon\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y) is surjective.

Since π1∞​(X)≅𝐙3\pi_{1}^{\infty}(X)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{3} by Proposition 8, it follows that π1∞​(Y)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y) is abelian.

We first determine the structure of π1∞​(Y)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y).

Claim. If Y∈𝒮0Y\in\mathscr{S}_{0} and π1∞​(Y)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y) is abelian, then π1∞​(Y)≅𝐙\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}.

Proof of the claim. By Proposition 10, π1∞​(Y)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y) admits the presentation

π1∞(Y)=⟨δ1,δ2,λ|δ1=[γ2,λ−1],δ2=[γ1,λ],[γ1,γ2]=1⟩,\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y)=\left\langle\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\lambda\;\middle|\;\delta_{1}=[\gamma_{2},\lambda^{-1}],\;\delta_{2}=[\gamma_{1},\lambda],\;[\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}]=1\right\rangle,

where γi=δidi\gamma_{i}=\delta_{i}^{\,d_{i}} for i=1,2i=1,2, following the notation of [26].

Since π1∞​(Y)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y) is abelian, the generators δ1\delta_{1}, δ2\delta_{2}, and λ\lambda commute pairwise. Hence [γ1,λ]=[δ1d1,λ]=1[\gamma_{1},\lambda]=[\delta_{1}^{d_{1}},\lambda]=1 and [γ2,λ−1]=[δ2d2,λ−1]=1[\gamma_{2},\lambda^{-1}]=[\delta_{2}^{d_{2}},\lambda^{-1}]=1. Using the defining relations, we obtain δ1=δ2=1\delta_{1}=\delta_{2}=1, and consequently γ1=γ2=1\gamma_{1}=\gamma_{2}=1. Hence the presentation simplifies to π1∞​(Y)=⟨λ⟩\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y)=\langle\lambda\rangle. Since there is no relation involving λ\lambda, it follows that π1∞​(Y)≅𝐙\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}. This proves the claim.

By definition, π1​(MY)=π1∞​(Y)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(M_{Y})=\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}, where MYM_{Y} denotes the 33-manifold at infinity of YY. By the discussion in Section 2.4, MYM_{Y} is prime. Hence, by [16, Lemma 3.13], MYM_{Y} is either irreducible or homeomorphic to S2×S1S^{2}\times S^{1}.

If MYM_{Y} is irreducible, then π1​(MY)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(M_{Y})\cong\mathbf{Z} contains an infinite cyclic normal subgroup, namely itself. Therefore, by the Seifert Fiber Space Theorem (Theorem 14), MYM_{Y} is Seifert fibered. If MY≅S2×S1M_{Y}\cong S^{2}\times S^{1}, then MYM_{Y} is also Seifert fibered. Thus, in either case, MYM_{Y} is a Seifert fibered 33-manifold.

Applying Neumann’s plumbing calculus [24] to the Seifert fibered manifold MYM_{Y}, we conclude that the boundary divisor DD of a smooth SNC compactification of YY is irreducible and isomorphic to ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1}. By Mumford’s presentation (Proposition 6), we have

π1∞(Y)≅⟨e∣eD2=1⟩,\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y)\cong\langle e\mid e^{\,D^{2}}=1\rangle,

where ee denotes the meridian corresponding to the unique irreducible component DD of the boundary divisor. Since π1∞​(Y)≅𝐙\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}, it follows that D2=0D^{2}=0; otherwise, π1∞​(Y)\pi_{1}^{\infty}(Y) would be finite.

On the other hand, since YY is affine, the boundary divisor is supported on an ample divisor. Hence D2>0D^{2}>0, a contradiction.

Therefore no finite surjective morphism f:𝐂∗×𝐂∗→Yf\colon\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}\rightarrow Y exists. Consequently, no smooth affine surface in the class 𝒮0\mathscr{S}_{0} is properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. ∎

The next step is to rule out smooth affine surfaces with an abelian fundamental group of rank 11 and positive Euler characteristic.

Proposition 16.

No smooth affine surface with fundamental group isomorphic to 𝐙\mathbf{Z} and positive Euler characteristic can be properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Proof.

Let X=𝐂∗×𝐂∗X=\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Assume, to the contrary, that there exists a finite surjective morphism f:X→Yf\colon X\rightarrow Y, where π1​(Y)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}, and e⁡(Y)>0e(Y)>0.

If deg⁡(f)=1\deg(f)=1, then ff is a finite birational morphism between smooth affine surfaces. Hence, by Zariski’s Main Theorem, ff is an isomorphism. This is impossible, since π1​(X)≅𝐙2\pi_{1}(X)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{2} whereas π1​(Y)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}. Therefore, deg⁡(f)>1\deg(f)>1.

Choose such a finite surjective morphism of minimal degree, and denote its degree by d>1d>1.

Claim. The induced homomorphism f∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Y)f_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Y) is surjective.

Proof of the claim. Suppose that f∗f_{\ast} is not surjective. By Remark 1, the morphism ff factors as g∘hg\circ h where g:Z→Yg\colon Z\rightarrow Y is a finite étale morphism, h:X→Zh\colon X\rightarrow Z is a finite surjective morphism, and h∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Z)h_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Z) is surjective. Since [π1(Y):f∗(π1(X))]<∞[\pi_{1}(Y):f_{\ast}(\pi_{1}(X))]<\infty (cf. [27]) and π1​(Y)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}, we obtain π1​(Z)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Z)\cong\mathbf{Z}. Moreover,

e⁡(Z)=deg⁡(g)​e​(Y)>0.e(Z)=\deg(g)\,e(Y)>0.

As deg⁡(h)<d\deg(h)<d, this contradicts the minimality of dd. Hence the claim follows.

Let p:Y′→Yp\colon Y^{\prime}\rightarrow Y be a connected 22-fold covering. Then Y′Y^{\prime} is again a smooth affine surface with π1​(Y′)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Y^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}. Since b0​(Y′)=1b_{0}(Y^{\prime})=1, b1​(Y′)=1b_{1}(Y^{\prime})=1, and bi​(Y′)=0b_{i}(Y^{\prime})=0 for i≥3i\geq 3, we have e⁡(Y′)=1−1+b2​(Y′)=b2​(Y′)e(Y^{\prime})=1-1+b_{2}(Y^{\prime})=b_{2}(Y^{\prime}). Furthermore,

e⁡(Y′)=deg⁡(p)​e​(Y)=2​e​(Y)≥2,e(Y^{\prime})=\deg(p)\,e(Y)=2e(Y)\geq 2,

so that b2​(Y′)≥2b_{2}(Y^{\prime})\geq 2.

Since f∗f_{\ast} is surjective, the covering pp pulls back to a connected finite covering, say q:X′→Xq\colon X^{\prime}\rightarrow X, via ff with the following commutative diagram

The morphism q:X′→Xq\colon X^{\prime}\rightarrow X is a finite unramified covering. Since every connected finite unramified covering of 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} is again isomorphic to 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} (Proposition 11), we have X′≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗X^{\prime}\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Consequently, b2​(X′)=1b_{2}(X^{\prime})=1, whereas b2​(Y′)≥2b_{2}(Y^{\prime})\geq 2. This contradicts Lemma 5(2) when applied to the finite surjective morphism f′:X′→Y′f^{\prime}\colon X^{\prime}\rightarrow Y^{\prime}. Hence no smooth affine surface with fundamental group isomorphic to 𝐙\mathbf{Z} and positive Euler characteristic can be properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. ∎

Corollary 17.

No smooth affine surface with an abelian fundamental group of rank 11 and positive Euler characteristic can be properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Proof.

Let YY be such a surface. Since π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) is a finitely generated abelian group of rank 11, using the structure theorem, we have π1​(Y)≅𝐙⊕T\pi_{1}(Y)\cong\mathbf{Z}\oplus T, where TT is a finite abelian group. Passing to the finite étale covering corresponding to the subgroup 𝐙↪𝐙⊕T≅π1​(Y)\mathbf{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{Z}\oplus T\cong\pi_{1}(Y) of finite index |T||T|, we obtain a smooth affine surface Y′Y^{\prime} with π1​(Y′)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Y^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z}. Moreover, e⁡(Y′)=|T|​e​(Y)>0e(Y^{\prime})=|T|\,e(Y)>0, as e⁡(Y)>0e(Y)>0. If YY were properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, then so would Y′Y^{\prime} using the earlier argument (see the proof of Proposition 13). This contradicts Proposition 16. This completes the proof. ∎

We are now in a position to complete the classification of smooth affine surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero that are properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}. Combining the preceding propositions with Kojima’s classification of strongly minimal affine surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero yields the following theorem.

Theorem 18.

Let YY be a smooth affine surface properly dominated by 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} with κ¯​(Y)=0\bar{\kappa}(Y)=0. Then YY is isomorphic to one of the following:

  1. (1)

    𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*};

  2. (2)

    Fujita’s surface H⁡[−1,0,−1]H[-1,0,-1].

Proof.

Let f:X→Yf\colon X\rightarrow Y be a finite surjective morphism, where X=𝐂∗×𝐂∗X=\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

If deg⁡(f)=1\deg(f)=1, then ff is a finite birational morphism between smooth affine surfaces. Hence, by Zariski’s Main Theorem, ff is an isomorphism. Therefore, Y≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗Y\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}, and we are done. Thus, we may assume that deg⁡(f)>1\deg(f)>1.

By Remark 1, we may factor ff as

where gg is a finite étale morphism, hh is a finite surjective morphism, f=g∘hf=g\circ h, and h∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Z)h_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Z) is surjective.

Since gg is a finite étale covering, π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is finite if and only if π1​(Y)\pi_{1}(Y) is finite. The latter is impossible by Proposition 13. Hence π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is infinite.

Let Z′Z^{\prime} be a strongly minimal affine surface obtained from ZZ by repeatedly contracting exceptional curves. Since logarithmic Kodaira dimension is preserved under such contractions, κ¯​(Z′)=κ¯​(Z)=0\bar{\kappa}(Z^{\prime})=\bar{\kappa}(Z)=0. Therefore, by Kojima’s classification [19, Table 1], the surface Z′Z^{\prime} is one of

O⁡(4,1),O⁡(2,2),O⁡(1,1,1),H⁡[−1,0,−1],H⁡[0,0].O(4,1),\quad O(2,2),\quad O(1,1,1),\quad H[-1,0,-1],\quad H[0,0].

Since the open immersion Z′↪ZZ^{\prime}\hookrightarrow Z induces a surjective homomorphism on fundamental groups, π1​(Z′)\pi_{1}(Z^{\prime}) is also infinite.

We first determine the intermediate surface ZZ. For this, the key step is to identify its strongly minimal model Z′Z^{\prime}.

Claim. Z′=Z≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗Z^{\prime}=Z\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}.

Proof of the claim. Since π1​(Z′)↠π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z^{\prime})\twoheadrightarrow\pi_{1}(Z) and π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is infinite, the surface Z′Z^{\prime} must have infinite fundamental group. By [19, Table 1], it follows that Z′Z^{\prime} is one of

O⁡(4,1),O⁡(2,2),O⁡(1,1,1),H⁡[−1,0,−1],H⁡[0,0].O(4,1),\quad O(2,2),\quad O(1,1,1),\quad H[-1,0,-1],\quad H[0,0].

Suppose that Z′Z^{\prime} is one of O⁡(4,1)O(4,1), O⁡(2,2)O(2,2), or H⁡[0,0]H[0,0]. Then π1​(Z′)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Z^{\prime})\cong\mathbf{Z} (see, [19, Table 1]). Since π1​(Z′)↠π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z^{\prime})\twoheadrightarrow\pi_{1}(Z), and π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is infinite, we obtain π1​(Z)≅𝐙\pi_{1}(Z)\cong\mathbf{Z}. Moreover,

e⁡(Z)=e⁡(Z′)+e⁡(Z∖Z′).e(Z)=e(Z^{\prime})+e(Z\setminus Z^{\prime}).

By [19, Lemma 1.4], the complement Z∖Z′Z\setminus Z^{\prime} is a (possibly empty) disjoint union of affine lines. Hence e⁡(Z)≥e⁡(Z′)>0e(Z)\geq e(Z^{\prime})>0, contradicting Proposition 16. Therefore, Z′Z^{\prime} is isomorphic to either O⁡(1,1,1)O(1,1,1) or H⁡[−1,0,−1]H[-1,0,-1].

We now show that Z=Z′Z=Z^{\prime}. Suppose, to the contrary, that e⁡(Z)>0e(Z)>0. Since h∗:π1​(X)→π1​(Z)h_{\ast}\colon\pi_{1}(X)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(Z) is surjective and π1​(X)≅𝐙2\pi_{1}(X)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{2}, the group π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is abelian. By Corollary 17, π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) cannot have rank one. Hence π1​(Z)≅𝐙2\pi_{1}(Z)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{2}. Since e⁡(Z)>0e(Z)>0, we have b2​(Z)≥2b_{2}(Z)\geq 2. On the other hand, by Lemma 5(2), the finite surjective morphism h:X→Zh\colon X\rightarrow Z implies b2​(Z)≤b2​(X)=1b_{2}(Z)\leq b_{2}(X)=1, a contradiction. Therefore e⁡(Z)=0e(Z)=0 and thus e⁡(Z′)=0e(Z^{\prime})=0 too. Since e⁡(Z)≥e⁡(Z′)e(Z)\geq e(Z^{\prime}) and equality holds if and only if Z∖Z′=∅Z\setminus Z^{\prime}=\varnothing, by [19, Lemma 1.4], we conclude that Z=Z′Z=Z^{\prime}.

Finally, from [19, Table 1], it follows that π1(H[−1,0,−1])=⟨y,t∣yty−1=t−1⟩\pi_{1}(H[-1,0,-1])=\langle y,t\mid yty^{-1}=t^{-1}\rangle, which is a nonabelian group, whereas π1​(Z)\pi_{1}(Z) is abelian as we observed above due to h∗h_{\ast} being surjective. Hence ZZ cannot be isomorphic to H⁡[−1,0,−1]H[-1,0,-1]. Therefore,

Z=Z′≅O⁡(1,1,1)≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗,Z=Z^{\prime}\cong O(1,1,1)\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*},

proving the claim.

Having identified ZZ, we now complete the proof. Since Z≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗Z\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} is an Eilenberg–MacLane K⁡(π,1)K(\pi,1)-space and g:Z→Yg\colon Z\rightarrow Y is a finite étale covering, it follows that YY is also an Eilenberg–MacLane K⁡(π,1)K(\pi,1)-space. By [9, Theorem 5.9], the only smooth affine Eilenberg–MacLane surfaces of logarithmic Kodaira dimension zero are 𝐂∗×𝐂∗\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*} and H⁡[−1,0,−1]H[-1,0,-1]. Hence

Y≅𝐂∗×𝐂∗orY≅H⁡[−1,0,−1],Y\cong\mathbf{C}^{*}\times\mathbf{C}^{*}\quad\text{or}\quad Y\cong H[-1,0,-1],

which completes the proof. ∎

Instructions for reporting errors
